utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can follow the proceedings in my mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances. Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and also good morning to my learned friends of the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, and I'm here together with co-counsel Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your colleagues. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours; good morning to my colleagues from the Prosecution. I am Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones I appear for the Defence of Mr. Naser Oric. With us is Ms. Adisa Mehic, our legal assistant, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam, and good morning to you and your colleagues. Any preliminaries? So let's bring the witness in. Now, the position is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have a technical problem here, which is that I'm not able to log on to the system. So although we have today's transcript, I don't have yesterday's and I'm not able to stop and scroll up. We've notified technical support and I think they're coming to help, but I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would come down and do it for you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm locked out of my account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can wait for them to fix it, because I think it's important. I mean, it's important for us, let alone for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, I can go ahead with this: I calculated the time that you used yesterday, that you used yesterday for your cross-examination, which of course does not include the time we used and the time lost on this and on that and of course the time used by the Defence. And you have already used 2.45 minutes from the five hours that we gave you. And we are not going to give you a minute more than the five hours, because we need also time ourselves to put questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, Mr. Jones, can I go ahead with the usual preliminaries? Yes, good morning to you, Mr. Dedic. Welcome back. We hope that this will be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We hope this will be your last day with us, I mean in this case, and that you will then be able to go back home. I hope you have had enough time to rest, and in fact my first question to you is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- whether you are feeling okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whether you are rested and whether we can continue. Yes. Has the problem been fixed?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's being fixed, but I think we can proceed for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The moment you need to stop, please do let me know straight away and we will stop. Cross reference to previous transcripts is always important. Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Wubben: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dedic.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will proceed on the questions I put to you yesterday, and we'll continue with the issue of the subregion. Yesterday you gave evidence about the meeting in which the subregion was decided upon, about the documents regarding that decision, and you gave evidence about your opinion that your position was that it was a very good idea and the reason why. I will turn now to the transcripts of the hearing of two days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So here we -- let's see if we encounter the first problem. Two days ago, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It looks like I'm getting there. If you'd give me 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Take as much time as you require on this. Sorry, Mr. Wubben, but I know you will understand that we should do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I have yesterday's transcript now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not yesterday's. He said two days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have that as well. I have all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Wubben. See if it's the case of starting again. And your question was as follows: "I will proceed on the questions I put to you yesterday, and we will continue with the issue of the subregion. Yesterday you gave evidence about the meeting in which the subregion was decided upon, about documents regarding that decision, and you gave evidence about your opinion that your position was that it was a very good idea and the reason why." And then you said you were going to turn to this transcript of two days ago. So you're invited to do that and proceed with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Transcript of two days ago, 12th of October, you gave evidence to the Court, and I quote: "When --" it's, for the record, page 33, line 3: "When communications were practically interrupted between Konjevic Polje, Cerska, and Skugrici. It's practically impossible ..." And page 35, upon the question: "When you described the reasons for the impossibility of the subregion beginning to function ..." your answer to the main reason for that was, and I quote line 17: "Precisely so. The main reason was the total isolation of these areas; they were cut off from each other." Do you recall, Mr. Dedic?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it your evidence that the lack of communication stood in the way of the implementation of the subregion? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will move to another issue, Your Honours. It's a video clip, P329. It's in the transcripts as well on hard copy, transcript 1. It's the interview of Naser Oric, page 7. Your Honour, something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I heard a bang, but I don't know what fell. What was that? They're supposed to dismantle this courtroom in due course, but it's being taken care of spontaneously.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So to repeat, P329, a video clip, transcript on hard copy is page 7, and the video clip will start at 2 hours, 33 minutes, 85 seconds. It will take one or two minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not to correct you that much, but it's 58 seconds and not 85 seconds. Please let's not invent any new chronological terms --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- and calculations. Yes. Let's move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "[Voiceover]... organised in Suceska, the Suceska territory and Tuzla, then amongst the houses where they were staying, the people -- the fighters who came to take part in the attack would then be accommodated in these various houses. In other words, two or three would stay in each house, so they'd have somewhere to sleep before the attack. "Usually if fighters came from one local area to another to help fight off an attack, for example, and if they stayed over overnight, then usually they would be put up with those local civilians. And usually the civilians, in terms of food or whatever, would give them whatever they had. "So that they would know, for example, which houses they could go to after they went up to the front lines during the day, which houses they could go to to get food. Of course, as the soldiers were making their preparations, the civilians were making their preparations too. As they had soldiers in their houses, they would hear where the first attack was going to be and then they would also make their preparations then to go up there, looking for food. "And however much we tried to protect that information of what we were going to do, we couldn't because we didn't have barracks and the soldiers were sleeping amongst the civilians in their houses."

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dedic, did you recognise the person sitting at the -- apparently the end, from your position on this picture, near the door?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm getting closer now. I think that is Mr. Oric, Mr. Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Naser Oric gave an interview, and in this interview he stated in this clip, this footage, that: "Usually if fighters came from one local area to another to help fight off an attack..." and then further on, "stayed overnight with civilians giving shelter." Did you hear that explanation?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I hear this speech, this particular morning, in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I mean is: Did you hear that Naser Oric was speaking about the fact that fighters usually came from one local area to another to help fight off an attack? Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that. I heard him saying that. But I did not quite understand which areas he was talking about. He probably knows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that fighters from Naser Oric, if so, came from one area to another to help fighting off an attack?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I were the witness, I wouldn't be able to answer this question, Mr. Wubben. What do you mean exactly? Because you're saying: "Are you familiar with the fact that fighters from Naser Oric, if so, came from one area to another to help fighting off an attack?" Are you referring to the fighters under the command of Naser Oric going from where they are to help fighting in another area? Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I give an example; to help off fighters, armed units, or groups in the Cerska area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer this first: What Mr. Wubben wants to know from you is whether you are aware of members of Oric's group, fighters in Oric's group, travelling to other areas to assist in the fight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is a fact that I'm unaware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you gave evidence of fighters helping out each other, groups helping out each other, and the need for it in the Cerska area. Did those fighters also go to other areas to help fighting off an attack?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fighters from Cerska, as far as I know, helped each other out in the territory of Cerska, and we also helped armed groups from Konjevic Polje, and vice versa. I don't know whether fighters from Konjevic Polje could ever have gone to Srebrenica. That is something I don't know about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the question is about other areas, and you gave at least evidence about the fact that fighters from Cerska were helping out an attack, helping off an attack related to Kravica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a small correction of the transcript. The witness said: "I don't know whether fighters from Cerska could go to Srebrenica," whereas the transcript says "... fighters from Konjevic Polje could go to Srebrenica." The witness referred to fighters from Cerska. He doesn't know whether they could go to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Is that correct, Mr. Dedic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I just know facts about fighters from Cerska, so this pertains to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Sorry, Mr. Wubben. Perhaps you can repeat your question, and your question was -- anyway, you repeat it. The question, as I read it here, you told the witness: "But the question is about other areas, and you gave at least evidence about the fact that fighters from Cerska were helping out an attack, helping off an attack related to Kravica."

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Dedic, what's your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I spoke about that earlier on. Fighters from Cerska - with your permission, I'd like to repeat that - about 50 of them, and five to six fighters from Cerska, at the request of a gentleman from Glogova, went to Kravica to help Mr. Golic. And I said that it was our interest because we were often shelled from Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So you told so. But the question was related to the fact that not only the fighters from Cerska and Konjevic Polje helped out in their own area, but also outside that area, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you answer that question, Mr. Dedic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand the question. If possible, could it please be repeated? Because I don't really understand what you're getting at. It's not a precise question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question is, if you allow me, Mr. Wubben: It's being suggested to you that the fighters from Cerska and Konjevic Polje went out to help others, not only in their area but also outside their own area. Would you agree to that? Did I put your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I wish to repeat my answer to this question. Fighters from Cerska and fighters from Konjevic Polje did help each other out. I've repeated that several times. But the only fact that I am aware of when the fighters from Cerska went further away from Cerska and Konjevic Polje was on the 7th of January, 1993, when they were in Kravica. I don't know whether it's clear now what I've been trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dedic. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also gave evidence about the fact that Hamed Salihovic, as president of the subregion, War Presidency of the subregion, gave orders and that those orders were also addressed to Semso Halilovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I don't know Semso Halilovic. The first part of the question as to whether Hamed Salihovic had been appointed president of the War Presidency of the subregion is correct. That's correct. And I have already said that he issued orders. However, I don't know Semso Halilovic. I don't know who that person is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Salihovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Salihovic. I apologise, Mr. Dedic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Semso Salihovic in Cerska received orders from Hamed Salihovic?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Semso Salihovic told me that Hamed, as soon as he saw someone, immediately started issuing orders to that person. So in my personal opinion, he was behaving like someone who was superior to all the armed forces, and also in the civilian authorities, superior to everybody else. That was how I saw Mr. Salihovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it is still your testimony that the subregion can be qualified as an attempt, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was only an attempt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when I see your position in that regard, if there had been a system of couriers and radio communication, and that system permitted communication, then you agree that the subregion would have functioned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones. Sorry. I didn't notice you before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Simply I object to that question as a pure hypothetical. Those conditions didn't obtain and so it's not for this witness to answer whether or not they would have functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, because this witness has a specific idea about the fact that it was an attempt. He clarified it, he reasoned it, and he also gave evidence about the reasons why it didn't function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So then ask him whether, in his considered opinion, the lack of -- whether the failure of this attempt was due to the absence of radio communication, existence of couriers, or the existing system of rudimentary system of communication, if at all. Because the way you put it, it seeks an opinion based on basically nothing, you know. I mean, it is hypothetical as it is. If you invert the question, you can get the same result without putting a hypothetical question. I don't know if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will not repeat the question, because that is the same reflection as his own opinion about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it's not hypothetical. Was one of the reasons for the failure to establish the subregion due to the rudimentary system of communications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand the word "rudimentary." Could you explain it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, it's something which leaves much to be desired, a system of communications which is not functioning, which has got many defects, many defaults; it doesn't work. That's what I mean. In other words, my question is: In your considered opinion, was the failure to have this subregion ongoing at least partly due to the fact that there was no good communications system at one's -- at the disposal or at your disposal, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because, Your Honours, there was no system of communication. And as I said earlier, only on rare occasions did people manage to pass out of these enclaves, to get out, because of the fierce attacks. And in essence, nothing changed except that these ideas were bandied about and discussed and put down on paper. But people continued to live in isolation from each other. I don't know if I've been sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you satisfied with that, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In that way, we have avoided all hypothetical considerations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's based on a considered opinion. I thank you for your objection, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Dedic, there was no other main reason for the failure of the subregion apart of that lack of communication?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has just said fierce attacks as well. It's not open --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This is not open for him to ignore the answer he's just given. He said people -- only on rare occasions did people manage to pass out of the enclaves, so one reason is lack of regular access because of fierce attacks. So if the witness has given that reason, it's not open to Mr. Wubben to say so the only reason is lack of communication. That's not the answer the witness has given. I don't think it's open to him to ignore answers given by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In that respect you are right. Perhaps you can redraft your question, Mr. Wubben, and now ask the witness to give us a comprehensive reason why, in his opinion and in his considered opinion, the subregion idea or project did not materialise at all. One reason, you said, there was fierce fighting; another reason, you said, Mr. Dedic, was lack of adequate communication system in place. What else could there have been? And you're not -- I want you to answer that question based on proper considerations and not just suppositions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these past few questions have confused me. I wish to repeat, by your leave, because I've been repeating this like a parrot all along: Every day the isolation of these areas increased, so that even the three meetings I attended could barely be held. I had to go along the river Jadar with this group of people from Cerska, to my waist in water, by night, in darkness. We sat there by candlelight. It was a time when it was practically impossible to organise anything, let alone the subregion, to organise anything and to link up these enclaves, which were literally cut off from each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that comprehensive enough to you, Mr. Wubben, or for your purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. I will proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And thank you, Mr. Dedic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dedic, how much is the distance between Srebrenica and Cerska, in your estimation?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the distance along the road used in peacetime or the way that I used in 1993 to go to Srebrenica from Cerska?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The distance as the crow flies, please.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the crow flies, I don't know that. Along the road which is there, it's 37 kilometres. That's the road used in peacetime, for normal traffic. So it might be half that as the crow flies. But that's only in my estimation; it need not be correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In November 1992, it was possible to visit various meetings in Cerska by representatives from Srebrenica, isn't it? "Yes" or "no," or "I don't know," please.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I don't know what you mean by "various meetings." What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it so that you had various meetings in November in which also representatives from Srebrenica participated?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were meetings. They weren't various meetings. As I said, Mr. Salihovic would arrive from Srebrenica with two other people. They did this on three occasions. And only in connection with issues concerning the subregion. I don't know about any other meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Srebrenica TO possessed Motorolas and Ham radios at the time? I mean November and later 1992.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this, because I arrived in Srebrenica only in March 1993, after these areas had fallen. So I can neither deny nor confirm your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you haven't heard of such a facility when you arrived in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived in Srebrenica, that was when I learnt that there was a Ham radio station, yes. I knew where it was, because I tried to use it to get some information about my son, who was in Belgrade at the time. So I found this out only after I had arrived there, that there was a Ham radio station in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that Ham radio they had prior to your arrival or not?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I told you when I saw it. I know that previously Mr. Salihovic had asked us to send Senahid Babic, a man from Cerska, to be trained in Srebrenica -- or I apologise: To be trained in Konjevic Polje, where he would be met by a young man to train him to try and set up these communications. But whether it was there at the time, I'm not sure, but they did request a man to be trained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in fact it was also at that time that a Ham radio existed in Srebrenica; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We from Cerska did not establish any contact through this kind of means of communication, so I cannot affirm with certainty that it existed in that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not my question, Mr. Dedic. I will repeat it, that with a view to the contact regarding setting up a Ham radio linkage between Konjevic Polje and Srebrenica, it appears to be that at that time, at least in Srebrenica, there was a Ham radio?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Wubben, I can say it appears to have been there, just as you say. All I can say with certainty is that it did exist when I saw it. And Mr. Salihovic had probably not have asked for a man to be trained had it not been there. So I can assume it was, but I cannot assert it was there if I didn't see it. Had I ever used that system of communication from Cerska, then I could have confirmed this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose you can move to something different, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that Mr. Kadir Hamidovic several times arrived from Glogova in Skugrici or Cerska?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned that before. This happened on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it? Can you tell the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He arrived in Cerska on two occasions. Once it was just before Christmas, that is, before the 7th of January, 1993. And this was a time, as I said before, just before the 7th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other time he arrived in Cerska or Skugrici?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the second time. The first time was before that. It was in December. So his last arrival was just before Christmas, the 7th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for the record, December is December 1992.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About Ejub Golic, you gave evidence that Ejub Golic and his armed men managed to break through some Serb lines and link up with the population of Glogova in the area of Glogova Mountain; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did mention that before. Ejub Golic, with a group of armed men, was in the village of Cizmici, a part of the population of Glogova; also with a group of armed men, was in the area of Mount Glogova. In this period, he managed to break through some Serb lines and link up from Cizmici with a large group of refugees from Glogova in Mount Glogova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also true that Ejub Golic had sent people to other places to ask for assistance?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kadir Hamidovic told me about it when he arrived. He said he had sent men to other places to ask for assistance, because he was encircled and afraid that they were all in grave danger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What other places were these?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't mention other places, but other armed groups in Cerska, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he came to Cerska, didn't he? Mr. Kadir Hamidovic came to Cerska and told you that Ejub Golic had sent people to other places, asking for assistance. What other places? Can you give names, please?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat: Kadir Hamidovic arrived in Skugrici because his sister was married there, where I lived. He came to see her. And I met him along the way. And in my conversation with him, I heard that. Cerska and Skugrici are very close to each other, as we saw on the map. And I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. learned from him that Mr. Golic had sent men to ask for assistance from some other groups in Cerska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Semso Salihovic go to help with an armed group upon this invitation by Kadir Hamidovic?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Semso Salihovic, after that, came to Skugrici, where he asked for volunteers to go with him. And he went on the 7th of January, 1993, as I have already said, with a group of about 50 armed men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you were at that time on Mount Tumace, if I pronounce it correctly, Tumace, Mr. Dedic?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You pronounced it quite well, but it's not really a mountain; it's an elevation. But yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where exactly is Tumace? I know -- I'm aware that you showed various places on the map. Can we show you the map again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's D814.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And usher, you need to concentrate on the top left quarter of the map. Yes. And if the technicians could zoom in to where Macesi and Konjevic Polje, and of course focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And there you see it, Tumace.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Wubben, Tumace is here, where I'm pointing with a pointer now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So isn't it true that you and your armed men also helped out Semso Salihovic because you, with those armed men, were on Mount Tumace, and if there be any Serb attacks, you and the armed men could intervene on time and you could not be caught by surprise, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there with a group of armed men. In case there was an attack anywhere, we would not be surprised and we would be able to help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 7th of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 7th of January, it was snowy, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the snow was quite deep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that snow prevent Semso Salihovic and his armed group to attack Kravica that day?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, Mr. Semso Salihovic, as I said before, did not attack Kravica. He attacked a place called Siljkovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Semso Salihovic -- did the snow prevent him to attack Siljkovici?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had it prevented him, he wouldn't have succeeded in attacking them, so he obviously managed to get through somehow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it didn't prevent him?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't a ZIS cannon brought in from that area? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A ZIS was brought from that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the fighters, the armed group from Cerska area make use of that ZIS cannon afterwards?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was brought to Cerska. Whether it was used, I can neither confirm nor deny, because, as I already said on the first day of my testimony, we did not have a trained crew to man such weapons, artillery weapons and armour systems and so on. I'm not aware of this, so I can neither confirm nor deny it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had this cannon been transferred to another armed group, as far as you know, another area?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that from the 7th of January, columns of civilians went from Cerska to Kravica area?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the 7th January on, for the following ten days or so, columns of civilians, not only from Cerska but also from Skugrici and Konjevic Polje, moved towards Kravica and back from Kravica. Because there was snow, you could see the columns very well, because they stood out in the white snow, and you could see them moving in both directions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they, as well as the fighters, return together with food and supplies?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The civilians went there exclusively to find food. They did find food. Some even brought back cattle feed. Others brought back windows, doors, roof tiles, and other building materials, in order to try to repair their heavily damaged houses, which were damaged due to shelling. And it was winter. It was very cold. So they wanted to repair their dwellings and make them habitable for the winter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me make sure that you understood the question that was put to you. You have given us an answer as regards the civilians, but you were also asked whether fighters returned with food and supplies. Did fighters also, like civilians, return with food and supplies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't hear the first part of the question. Yes, yes, they did return with weapons and food supplies, like civilians, because food is something that neither civilians nor fighters had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Dedic. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far in the last half an hour, we discussed movement of people around the area from various places, and my question to you is that it should then be possible, whenever there is a need to move around, whenever there is a need to go from one area to another, then even given the fierce attack or the fierce threats, that movement is indeed possible, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, that question is far too vague, I'm afraid. The witness has been giving evidence about movement to Kravica, which is, as we all know, I hope, is in Bratunac municipality. Earlier there have been questions about Srebrenica municipality. I'm sure Mr. Wubben doesn't mean to confuse the witness so that his answer appears to apply to Srebrenica municipality, but referring to "various places" is vague enough that it could later be stretched to include Srebrenica municipality. If we could stick with the municipalities which have been specifically mentioned. "Various places," how far does that extend; Tuzla, Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Basically, my problem with your question, Mr. Wubben, is that I agree with Mr. Jones that it is somewhat vague and somewhat confusing as well, or possibly confusing. You say: "So far in the last half-hour we have discussed movement of people around the area from various places, and my question to you is that it should then be possible, whenever there is a need to move around, whenever there is a need to go from one area to another, that even given the fierce attack and fierce threats, that movement is indeed possible, isn't it?" Basically, what Mr. Wubben is trying to convey to you is this: He has given you various instances and asked you about various instances where both civilians and fighters were moving from one place to another in an area where there was fierce fighting and at times also deep snow, as you put it. And it's being put to you now that the logical conclusion that one could come to is that in spite of the negative conditions that prevailed at the time, one could still move around if one wanted to. What I require from Mr. Wubben is to make it clear which area he is restricting his question to, because the witness, I suppose, can only answer in relation to the area that he was familiar with and not beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: But he might also learn from other people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then ask him, okay. So divide the question into two.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The first question that you need to answer, therefore, you need to limit to the area that you were familiar with, first and foremost, and then Mr. Wubben will ask you a second question afterwards. Would you agree with the suggestion that is being put to you that in spite of all these difficulties, in spite of the fierce fighting, in spite of the negative conditions on the ground, on the terrain, one could still move from one area to another, in your area? Would you agree to that supposition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, by your leave, I'd rather say "had to," because the choice was between finding food, or rather, just having the food that you had for a few days, or, on the other hand, risking even your life to go out and get some food and survive for longer. As for the other part of the question, I don't know. I don't know whether people from Srebrenica went, or from some other places. I saw people who went and came back to the areas that I mentioned, the areas where I lived. I don't know whether I've been clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. To me, you have been clear enough, but it's not my question; it's Mr. Wubben's question. So I don't know if he is happy with your answer or whether he wants to explore this area any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I mean: You gave evidence, Mr. Dedic, about going to Tumace from Cerska, and backwards. You gave evidence of going to Konjevic Polje from Cerska, and backwards. You gave evidence of going to Siljkovici and backwards. You gave evidence about going to Cerska and Skugrici from Glogova, and backwards. You gave evidence going from Srebrenica to Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and backwards. You gave evidence of going through Serb lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I think the witness should be asked -- it wasn't quite clear whether you asked him whether he went between all these villages, to all these places, or whether other people also have been able to move between these places which you had mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will add a further clarification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave evidence about the movement between those places, going and backwards, by people, and you confirmed that these people were able to travel between those places, even given those dreadful circumstances. Not by yourself, but you witnessed it. Now, have there been other movements that you are aware of by persons in other areas, from November 1992?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, I would appreciate it if you would put short questions to me. Then it's easier for me to answer. This way, you put several questions to me in one, and I'm not in a position to follow all of it. So could you please put one question at a time to me and tell me precisely what it is that you want me to say so that I could answer properly. This way, you confuse me, and perhaps I don't give you the right kind of answer, and then again we just waste time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dedic, let me put, then, a short question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you go straight to examples, instances. I'll just invent two names, for example. Whether he is aware of any traffic of persons, movements of persons, from, for example, Drinjaca to Lijesanj, or from Lijesanj to Cerska or Cajici, or something like that. Because otherwise, it's too vast. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's a vast area, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's also -- I mean, he will have to exercise a lot of mental fatigue to try and remember all the possibilities that there could be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I gave you, Mr. Dedic -- if I may continue, Your Honour. I gave you an overview of travelling by people around various areas by naming places, and I will repeat, and you can confirm whether it was possible or not, as you witnessed. And let's take the time from November 1992 up to January 1993. Did you witness that someone was able to travel from Cerska to Tumace elevation? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether some people did, but I came to Tumace on the 7th of January with a group of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, with a group of people, came there. So, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You witnessed that it was possible to travel to Siljkovici from Konjevic Polje and Cerska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Travelling from Cerska via Konjevic Polje to Siljkovici was possible, because the group I mentioned did arrive there. So on the basis of that, it was possible, in very difficult conditions, but it was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Dedic, I understand that it was difficult, but the question is very plain and clear, I think: It was possible. Then you can -- then it will be sufficient to answer it by "yes," if you can. And also backwards from Siljkovici to Cerska and Konjevic Polje; is that true?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Please. People left Cerska, went to Siljkovici, and came back to Cerska from Siljkovici. Of course, not everybody. Some got killed. But the survivors came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That was also a yes, and a yes will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know what you're going to say. If he wants to explain, obviously he needs to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's not simply that. If Mr. Wubben is saying is it possible to travel back and forth for people, and people get killed, and obviously it's not possible because they've been killed and they don't return, then that's part of the relevant answer to the question. Just to ignore the dead people and say, well, for those who survived, it was possible. And I don't think one can say it's simply yes or no. If people are in extremis crawling through the snow to get back, that's surely relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These are not instances where one could board a bus or a taxi and go from one place to another. I mean, we're talking of difficult circumstances and difficult terrain, in a time of conflict, armed conflict. I mean, we found it difficult sometimes to travel Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ourselves during the on-site visit in certain areas, in peacetime, but with armoured cars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition, it was also possible to travel from Cerska to Glogova, or to be specific, from Glogova to Cerska, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not possible to travel. I've mentioned to you that one single man that I know of who managed to go there and come back alive. Mr. Wubben, travelling, in my books, means that we pack our things, go at leisure, that we're sure that we can come back safely. That's what travel means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I mean is to make the journey, to make the trip, with a certain aim. So if we can include that in your information, if it is possible to make the trip to a certain area. Then that should inform the Trial Chamber. The additional -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, I would not say that this is a proper road, because roads that existed before the war could not be used. So people went through the wild, if I can put it that way. They went through places where animals moved around otherwise. These are not proper roads for communication, because not a single road that existed from before could have been used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Kadir Hamidovic was able to make that trip in December and January, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And a shell would fall into a group of 20 people, and some would survive and others would get killed. There are some people who went to Tuzla, hundreds of kilometres, and not everybody was killed. Some managed to survive. So there is not a single case that could prove that there was proper communication there and that it was possible to communicate. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And people were also able to travel to Tuzla; is that your testimony, at the time?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that time. Even earlier and sometimes later, some people from Cerska, Konjevic Polje, or Srebrenica, in wartime, somehow managed to reach Tuzla alive, although it's a much longer way, but there are some who survived the trip, whereas there were many others who, unfortunately, did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually, let's -- I mean, go ahead as much as you like, Mr. Wubben, but in reality, the truth of the situation is what the witness has told us, that the normal roads and streets could not be used, but one could find his way through the woods, through the forests, across rivers. If one, I suppose, wanted to go to Belgrade and walk it all the way, one could still do it. So at the end of the day, it's a question of how you manage to find your way and whether you would be lucky in getting there at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was addressing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. I mean, I'm not stopping you. Please don't misunderstand me. But in reality, I think you are labouring on a point that it is pretty much laboured sufficiently already. I mean, the witness is telling you when people wanted to go to Kravica to attack, well, of course we got there. When people wanted to go to Cerkovici [phoen], of course we got there. When people -- not we. I'm saying whoever needed to go there and wanted to go there, went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And many died and never came back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And many died in the process. Many got there, but never made it back as well, even though they were still alive after the fighting. So this is the truth of the -- the unfortunate truth of the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you ask, could you cross from Cerska to Srebrenica, or could you even walk through Serb-occupied territory, if you were lucky and you used your brains and you have got luck on your side, yes, of course you can do it. And you know the way, of course, which is the most important thing. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And in addition -- thank you, Your Honour, for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition, Mr. Dedic, when it comes to casualties and killings and all these threats on the way during such a trip, it is so that the armed units, the armed men, or the fighters familiar with the area has a greater chance to survive than untrained civilians, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, could you please put a specific question to me? You've given me a description -- actually, I don't see what I could say to that. Could you please put a concrete question to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the question is clear enough, Mr. Dedic. If Mr. Wubben wants any assistance, I will assist him. But otherwise, I think it's clear enough. You are being asked to make a comparison with those people who were armed and familiar with the area, with the terrain, and those civilians who were not familiar with the terrain, and he is asking you whether you would agree that those who were armed and familiar with the terrain had a better chance to survive than those civilians who were not armed and were not familiar with the terrain. This is a simple question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, yes. It was easier. It was easier, to my mind, for civilians to go, because they went behind armed men, whereas the largest number of civilians, people who went to Kravica and back, went when the Serb forces were repelled from Kravica. They took the road from Konjevic Polje to Kravica. And then, after the Serb forces were repelled from Kravica, they were quite far away from Kravica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: A moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I meant was not the chance to get killed when it comes to columns of civilians and fighters accompanying them, but what I mean is when fighters or civilians would like to move within the area, given the threats and the possible attacks, that the fighters, knowing the area and having the assistance, have less chance to get killed than civilians who are untrained or do not know the area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The assistance of who?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's clear enough, Mr. Jones. Leave it. Let him answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not correct that the civilians were not familiar with the area. All those civilians live in the area and they knew the area as well as the fighters did, except that some of these people who were military-able had a rifle. However, say his wife knew equally well where Kravica was, just like her husband did, except she didn't have a rifle and she was not in the armed group. So civilians were very familiar with the area, because they lived there for years - in the area, that is - so they knew it very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that some fighters had been trained in the army, in the JNA army, the compulsory training? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether all members of these groups that we referred to earlier on had done their military service in the JNA, because there were some young people. So I'm not sure from that point of view that everybody had done their military service. As for the level of training, how trained people were, I cannot be the judge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move to another issue. Are you aware that there was a prison in Cerska, if so, at the time, I mean, by the end -- the second half of 1992/beginning 1993?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't quite understand. What are you asking me about? What -- did what exist in Cerska? I didn't hear a word. Was there what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the translation not functioning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine that there is a problem with interpretation, and I see Ms. Vidovic confirming that. So you need to repeat your question, please, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there at the time a prison in Cerska, if so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In November 1992 or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From October until the end or -- are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the existence of any kind of prison in Cerska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any building used as a detention centre or occasionally used as such?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you again referring to the area of Cerska?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the buildings that I knew in Cerska were used exclusively for housing the population, for the accommodation of people who lived there and for the accommodation of a large number of refugees who were there. Warehouses, apartments of teachers, the elementary school, I'm only aware of the premises where people lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any Serb prisoners being held somewhere in Cerska or the neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any such fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A couple of days ago, you were shown a report from a chief of the SJB, Mr. Radomir Bijelanovic. Are you familiar with that name?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Radomir, Rade, Bijelanovic. I know the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his function at the time?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What time are you referring to specifically? What period of time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The end of January. Sorry. The end of 1992, January 1993.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for his exact position at that time, I don't know. I don't know what he did at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he, let's say, in the beginning of 1993, involved in exchange of Serb prisoners for Muslims? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of exchange you are referring to. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whenever it's convenient, it's convenient for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a 30-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I ask the usher to show the witness Exhibit D825. Your Honours, that's my last exhibit for today to discuss.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dedic, you're shown a document, a combat order by the Drina Corps command, and shown to you in an earlier stage by the Defence. Do you have that in front of you, Mr. Dedic, that document?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document, in paragraph 2, is read as being the last sentence, and I quote: "Be in a state of readiness for defence immediately, and for attack by 0600 hours on the 24th of January, 1993." Did you follow?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we move to the following page, under paragraph 7, the third line, and it might be, in English, second line: "Establish communications by 0530 hours on the 24th of January, 1993." Did you follow?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doesn't that mean, as I put it to you also yesterday, that it appears to be that the Drina Corps tried to prevent any interception of radio communication prior to the attack?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the Drina Corps wanted to do with this, I don't know, and I wouldn't wish to comment on it. That's up to the person who drew up this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I asked you a question. I asked you: Isn't it so that the Drina Corps in this way tried to prevent any interception from the enemy prior to the attack?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, if he tells you yes or if he tells you no, it is not going to change anything. This is a submission that you will make later on. Whatever the witness is going to answer to that question is not going to change the reality of the situation. Why would one first say we will start with the attack at 6.00 or be prepared to start the attack at 6.00, establish connections at 5.30, and before that, as we saw yesterday in some document - I don't know if it's this one or another one - the communication was to be by courier? I mean, one draws one's conclusion. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's why I asked the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but the witness is not going to provide you with an answer. He gave you the only answer that any witness would give you. I mean, whoever gave that order knows best.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will proceed on this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 1, on the first page, Witness, I will quote the first part of it: "In counter-offensive operations the enemy has managed to take part of the territory that had been controlled by Corps units and has inflicted serious losses on our units (the sector of Sasa, Kravica, Mount Glogova, Skelani, Setihovo - the general Rudo sector)." My question to you is: You earlier stated that the content of this document is correct, that what's mentioned in this order in the connection of the counter-offensives, that it is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The part of the document that mentions our forces, that is, the Muslim forces, managing to take territories in counter-offensive operations, that is, Kravica and Mount Glogova, that is correct, yes. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these counter-offensive operations have been quite successful, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they were successful or not, that's a very broad question. But we did manage to push back the Serb forces from Kravica, and according to what I was told by the man we often mentioned from Glogova Planina, the -- well, as for the other areas mentioned here, I don't know what happened there. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as far as the enemy, as quoted, has managed to take part of the -- parts of it, the operation was quite successful, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, I wish to repeat: It is only the area of Kravica, which we have often mentioned, and the area of Mount Glogova, where Mr. Golic's armed forces managed to link up, that one can say that the counter-offensive was successful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those counter-offensives, as far as you know and are aware of being successful, those counter-offensives must have been the result of combined planning and communication from the Muslim forces involved; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to mention once again that I don't remember anyone ever planning anything in connection with the activities of the Muslim forces. What happened was the collecting of volunteers. But I never saw any plans, nor do I know anyone who drew up any kind of plan in connection with counter-offensive operations by our forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I put it to you that these are true facts as I will explain: Isn't it also true that these counter-offensive operations by Muslim forces were the outcome of a unified joint command?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, that's your standpoint. My standpoint is well known. I've reiterated it more than once. The participation of the forces from Skugrici and Cerska is all I know about. I don't have any information about any other forces, how many there were and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I also will put it to you that communicating was possible via couriers and radio communication throughout the subregion area. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do these counter-offensive operations and being successful also mean that your reason for the subregion not functioning had been removed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: First, the witness hasn't accepted that these operations were successful. He was asked about that and he said that wasn't something which he could affirm. So Mr. Wubben can put it to the witness again if he wants, they were successful, but the witness has answered that. And for the rest of it, I really don't see that a clear question is emerging from what Mr. Wubben was saying. The witness has asked and we've asked for clear questions to be put to the witness and that's very far it from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones' remark that the witness has not conceded to you, Mr. Wubben, that these counter-offensives were successful is a correct observation. And then therefore I would suggest that you rephrase your question, putting it to the witness in conformity with what he has already stated in regard to your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should then go back to the transcript. In my opinion, he admitted at least so far as he knows about Kravica and Mount Glogova, that these operations have been successful. I have to check that in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said -- when you asked him -- it's line 4 on page 36, at least on mine, because sometimes I get the impression that it varies from monitor to monitor. "So these counter-offensive operations have been quite successful, isn't it?" That's what you asked him. And he said: "Whether they were successful or not, that's a very broad question. But we did manage to push back the Serb forces from Kravica, and according to what I was told by the man we often mentioned from Glogova Planina -- well, as for the other areas mentioned there, I don't know what happened there."

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Further, Your Honour, I put the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And then you asked: "But as far as the enemy, as quoted, has managed to take part of it, the operation was quite successful, isn't it?" "Mr. Wubben, I wish to repeat, it's only the area of Kravica, which we have often mentioned, and the area of Mount Glogova, where Mr. Golic's armed forces managed to link up, that one can say the counter-offensive was successful."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's one specific counter-offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It's not one specific --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's two. Glogova, Mount Glogova, and Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So the question can be confined to that specific counter-offensive, and do those counter-offensives, that success, does that show that the subregion was functioning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree 100 per cent. I mean, you can split or rephrase your question, provided -- whichever way you like, provided it reflects the answer that the witness has given you before to the question of whether he considers -- because you didn't ask him about the counterattacks in Kravica and Mount Glogova only. The document 825 mentions Sasa, mentions five or six places; Skelani, Setihovo and the general Rudo sector, plus Sasa. So if you want, you can divide the question into two and try to see what information the witness can give you, keeping in mind that he's only given you a direct answer with regard to two counterattacks and not five, one of which seems to be the general Rudo sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dedic, with a view to the successful counter-offensives regarding Kravica and Glogova, Mount Glogova, doesn't that mean that your reason for the subregion not functioning has been removed?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never said that was one of the reasons, because I wish to state that both these areas were very quickly retaken by the Serb forces. This was only a brief period in which the Muslim forces controlled these areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if the other sectors mentioned in paragraph 1 of the combat order are also being successful indeed, doesn't that also mean that your reason for the subregion not functioning had been removed?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you a direct answer to that question. I know, for example, that Rudo is somewhere in Eastern Bosnia and has nothing to do with this area. So I couldn't respond to that question. The only Rudo I know is a small place far away from Srebrenica, somewhere in Eastern Bosnia, in the direction of Visegrad or Cajnice or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben. Is there re-examination, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead. Re-examined by Ms. Vidovic:

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, would the usher please show the witness P581 again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dedic, in your testimony of yesterday, you responded to a number of questions put to you by the Prosecutor concerning your request to be admitted to active military service in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to have a rank conferred upon you. You have the document before you. Please take a look at it and tell me, first of all, whether or not you agree that this is a form which is the same for all members of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, regardless of the area they come from, if you're aware of this.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have seen a certain number of forms in the possession of members of other groups from Tuzla. I've seen this form, and this, as far as I can tell, is identical, this form was identical everywhere. There was no other kind of form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please now see whether I have correctly read out the title: "Request for joining the active military service of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and promotion to rank." Have I read this out correctly?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that this document, on the 20th of February, 1994, was only an application to be received into the active military service of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was only an application, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, then, that until the 20th of February in 1994, at least, you had not joined the active military service of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that you are only now requesting to join it; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. I was received into active military service in September 1997, or 1998, I'm not quite sure. I'm sure it's either the September of 1997 or 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Please take a look at number 40. What does it say under number 40? And take a good look, please. Do you agree that it says "Date of putting oneself at the disposal of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, state the organ to which you reported." Is this what it says here?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's possible that the English translation contains something else, but this is what I'm reading out in the original.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this correct, Witness?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you filled in next to this, it says: "On the 5th of April, 1992," does this mean that it was then that you simply put yourself at the disposal of someone?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I wish to say again that this was a small group of people trying to work out what to do to avoid war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now look at 41, please. Yesterday, testifying about this part, you explained, more than once, what the armed groups looked like in your area as of the 15th of April, 1992. I won't go into it again. Please don't repeat your explanation, so as to avoid wasting time. But I will ask you the following: The situation on the ground as of the 6th of April and onwards, throughout 1992, was this at that point of time the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina or were they simply armed groups of the people of Cerska offering spontaneous resistance to the enemy?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although I've repeated it more than once, I wish to repeat again: These were smaller or larger armed groups of the population, of people who lived locally. There were no military formations in that area in the spring and summer of 1992 up until the fall of these areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The main point of my question was whether these groups were offering resistance spontaneously, whether they were self-organised or whether they were acting under orders as part of larger formations.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they never acted under orders. All their activities were exclusively voluntary and they were never linked up into some kind of chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to clarify: Throughout 1992 until the fall of Cerska, did you have any contact with the units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and did you get any kind of help or support from them?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. All the assistance I mentioned earlier was among the local groups acting in the area of Konjevic Polje and Cerska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any orders in the Cerska area from any higher commands of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such thing. Never did I see any such order with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you write reports? You explained that you were in Skugrici as part of one such group. Did you send reports from this group in Skugrici to anyone until the fall of Cerska?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember ever writing reports or sending them to anyone, because nobody ever requested any kind of report. Everything that happened, happened within that armed group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now please look at the last page of this document, where it says: "Opinion and proposal of the commander of the 8th Operative Group Srebrenica." And I'm going to read out a sentence to you, where the commander says: "Ejub Dedic was engaged in purchasing and reselling armament and ammunition. He was organising people in the region of Skugrici, Vlasenica, and distinguished himself as an organiser of village guards." Please, yesterday you clarified this fact sufficiently about weapons. The point of my question is the following: Do you see this here? In his alleged opinion and proposal, he says: "He was organising people in the region of Skugrici, Vlasenica, and distinguished himself as an organiser of village guards." Now, please, what it says here, what I read out to you, does it correspond to the facts that you talked about yourself, that you said that you originally entered into the form that was given to you by the official of Bosnia-Herzegovina before this person insisted that you correct the information entered?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of this information with organised groups. However, at the explicit insistence of this person, he asked for the entries to be made as they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And in relation to that: This man who gave you the form, this request to join active military service, was he an authorised official? Was this a person who was authorised to work with these forms or questionnaires, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, he was not authorised, probably, because he was carrying a lot of these papers around and he was handing them out to everyone, and he was walking by us and giving out these forms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The point of my question is the following: He was a person who worked with these papers, and did you actually give him correct information about what you did in Cerska and what this unit of yours was like?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote the first version correctly. I wrote correctly about everything that happened. However, later on, he looked at that document and he did not accept that part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he actually suggest to you what you were supposed to write?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. He said that it couldn't be put that way, the way you put it, although it is probably so. It has to be written this other way.
